cues.text: Let us turn now to the second topic in this chapter: Scrum.
Scrum is a lightweight framework for complex product work.
Notice the word framework.
Scrum is not a detailed step-by-step procedure; it gives a light structure within which a team does its work.
It is based on empiricism, which means that decisions are made from what has actually been observed, and it rests on three ideas: transparency, inspection, and adaptation.
Transparency means the work and its progress are visible to those who need to see them.
Inspection means the team looks honestly at that work and its results.
Adaptation means the team changes course when the inspection shows something needs to change.
Scrum also values five things: commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage.
Now let us meet the Scrum Team.
It includes three kinds of people.
First, the Product Owner, who maximises value and manages the Product Backlog.
Second, the Scrum Master, who helps establish Scrum and helps the team be effective.
Third, the Developers, who create a usable Increment, and who plan and adapt their own work.
Two points are often misunderstood.
The Product Owner is one accountable person, not a committee.
Many people may offer input, but one person is accountable.
And the Scrum Master is not necessarily a line manager.
The role is about helping the team with Scrum and effectiveness, not about managing people in a reporting hierarchy.
Next, the Sprint.
A Sprint is of fixed length, one month or less, and it contains the Scrum events.
Let us walk through them in order.
The first is Sprint Planning.
It answers three questions.
Why: this is the Sprint Goal.
What: this is the selected Product Backlog items for the sprint.
And how: this is the delivery plan for getting that work done.
The second is the Daily Scrum.
This is a fifteen-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan.
It is not a status report to a manager.
It exists for the Developers themselves.
The third is the Sprint Review.
Here the team inspects the Increment and its outcomes together with stakeholders, and then adapts future work based on what is learned.
The fourth is the Sprint Retrospective.
Here the team inspects its own process and plans improvements to quality and effectiveness.
Now the artifacts and their commitments.
There are three pairs.
The Product Backlog goes with the Product Goal.
The Sprint Backlog goes with the Sprint Goal.
And the Increment goes with the Definition of Done.
Some important clarifications.
Product Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, not a formal event.
The Definition of Done establishes a quality standard across increments, whereas acceptance criteria are specific to an individual item; keep those two apart.
Also, a usable Increment can be delivered before the Sprint Review.
The review is not a mandatory release approval step.
Finally, consider the example sprint, in the tracking context.
The product goal is reliable tracking.
The sprint goal is to display the accurate current parcel state.
To pursue this, the team selects stories within its capacity, and clarifies acceptance tests.
It then plans the design, the API, the user interface, and the testing.
During the sprint it inspects progress daily.
At the end it demonstrates the increment, captures stakeholder feedback, and improves its process.
One last caution: do not treat the sprint backlog as unchangeable.
The team can adapt it as it learns, but must do so without undermining the Sprint Goal.
